title: Sieve Principle: IE for 2 and 3 Bad Sets
content: The sieve_two theorem proves |U \ (A ∪ B)| = |U| - |A| - |B| + |A ∩ B| (in ℤ). The proof uses `card_sdiff_add_card_eq_card` (to remove A ∪ B from U) and `card_union_add_card_inter` (the IE formula for A ∪ B), then closes with `omega`. Working over ℤ (not ℕ) avoids underflow issues: subtraction can go negative in intermediate steps. The 3-set version adds a distributivity step: (A ∪ B) ∩ C = (A ∩ C) ∪ (B ∩ C), proved by `tauto` on the logical equivalence.
mathContext:
$$|U \setminus (A \cup B)| = |U| - |A| - |B| + |A \cap B|$$
$$|U \setminus (A \cup B \cup C)| = |U| - |A| - |B| - |C| + |A\cap B| + |A\cap C| + |B\cap C| - |A\cap B\cap C|$$

title: Euler Totient: φ(pq) = (p-1)(q-1) via Multiplicativity
content: The theorem totient_two_primes proves φ(pq) = (p-1)(q-1) for distinct primes p, q. The proof: first establishes that p and q are coprime using `hp.coprime_iff_not_dvd` (a prime p doesn't divide q, since the only divisor of q that equals p would require p = q, contradicting hpq). Then applies multiplicativity `Nat.totient_mul` and the prime totient formula `Nat.totient_prime`. This is the IE sieve explanation: out of pq elements, remove multiples of p (pq/p = q of them) and multiples of q (pq/q = p of them), then add back multiples of both (1 element).
mathContext:
$$\varphi(pq) = pq\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{q}\right) = (p-1)(q-1) \quad \text{for distinct primes } p, q$$
Sieve: $pq$ total - $q$ multiples of $p$ - $p$ multiples of $q$ + $1$ multiple of $pq$ $= pq - q - p + 1 = (p-1)(q-1)$.

title: Surjection Counting: IE over k Bad Events
content: The surjection count formula counts functions f: [n] → [k] with every element of [k] in the image. The 'bad' events are Bⱼ = {f: j ∉ image(f)}. By IE, |Surj(n,k)| = Σ_{j=0}^k (-1)^j C(k,j)(k-j)^n: the (-1)^j factor alternates, C(k,j) counts subsets of j excluded outputs, and (k-j)^n counts functions avoiding those j outputs. Special cases: surjection_n_1 (n→{1} is 1 surjection) and surjection_n_2 (n→{1,2} gives 2^n - 2 by inclusion-exclusion: all functions minus constant-1 and constant-2).

title: Derangements: Permutations with No Fixed Points
content: A derangement is a permutation σ: [n] → [n] with σ(i) ≠ i for all i. The IE formula: bad event Bᵢ = {σ: σ(i) = i}. By IE, D(n) = Σ_{k=0}^n (-1)^k C(n,k)(n-k)! = n! Σ_{k=0}^n (-1)^k/k!. The sequence {1,0,1,2,9,44,265,...} satisfies two recurrences: D(n) = (n-1)(D(n-1)+D(n-2)) (element n can go to any of n-1 non-fixed positions, and either element it displaces becomes or doesn't become a fixed point) and D(n) = n·D(n-1)+(-1)^n. All verified via native_decide.

title: Alternating Binomial Sum = 0 for n ≥ 1
content: The alternating binomial sum Σ_{k=0}^n (-1)^k C(n,k) = (1-1)^n = 0 for n ≥ 1 (by the binomial theorem). This is the 'empty IE' — the sum counts the number of elements in the empty set after subtracting all bad events. Verified computationally for n=1..10. This identity underlies why surjectionCount and derangements work: the IE formula, when applied to the full set of 'all events being bad', correctly returns 0.
mathContext:
$$\sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} = (1-1)^n = 0^n = 0 \quad \text{for } n \geq 1$$
This is the binomial theorem $(x+y)^n = \sum_k \binom{n}{k} x^k y^{n-k}$ at $x=-1, y=1$.

title: Divisor-Totient Identity: Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n
content: The divisor-totient identity states that the sum of Euler's totient over all divisors of n equals n. Proof via IE and multiplicativity: the integers 1,...,n can be partitioned by their GCD with n: for each divisor d, exactly φ(n/d) integers in {1,...,n} satisfy gcd(k,n)=d (namely multiples of d coprime to n/d). Summing over all divisors gives n. In Lean, this is a one-liner using Mathlib's `Nat.sum_totient`. The identity demonstrates that φ is a 'Dirichlet inverse' of the constant-1 function: if one applies Möbius inversion, φ = μ ∗ id.
mathContext:
$$\sum_{d \mid n} \varphi(d) = n$$
Partition proof: $\{1,\ldots,n\} = \bigsqcup_{d|n} \{k : \gcd(k,n) = d\}$, and $|\{k : \gcd(k,n)=d\}| = \varphi(n/d)$.

title: Stirling Numbers S(n,k) and Bell Numbers via IE
content: The Stirling numbers of the second kind S(n,k) count set partitions of {1,...,n} into k non-empty blocks. They are derived from surjections: S(n,k) = |Surj(n,k)| / k! (since each surjection corresponds to k! orderings of the k blocks). Bell numbers B(n) = Σ_{k=0}^n S(n,k) count total set partitions. Computed values: B(0)=1, B(1)=1, B(2)=2, B(3)=5, B(4)=15, B(5)=52. Verified by native_decide via the integer division of surjectionCount.
